CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS, AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEE Report #2022-2023-7 - INFORMATIONALFACULTY SENATE, November 17, 2022 Context and rationale: At the Faculty Senate meeting on September 29, 2022, Senate leadershipshared with the community a long list of administrative policies that had been recently approved bythe Administrative Policy Committee (APC).
Senators expressed concerns about the speed at whichpolicies were being developed/revised and approved, and about the opacity with which the APCseemed to be functioning (ambiguity in University Manual language about committee membership,lack of availability of a list of current members on any URI website, lack of details available to theuniversity community about APC vetting processes, etc.).
In response to the listing of the policies onthe agenda and the brief discussion that took place, Faculty Senate President Rice asked Senators andSenate standing committees to examine the policies closely and to invite colleagues across campus todo the same.

The purpose of these efforts is to engage the faculty in administrative policydevelopment and amendment processes, to correct potential errors or flaws in new or revisedadministrative policies (conflicts with the existing duly approved administrative or academic policiesin the University Manual, areas in which all impacts appear to not have been fully considered, orother flaws), and to improve the quality of administrative policies that are ultimately adopted by thecommunity.
In response to President Rice’s request, CBUM is devoting time during each meeting to review anddiscuss policies listed on the September Faculty Senate meeting agenda.
The main aim of our scrutinyis to identify potential errors or conflicts as they relate to the duly approved statutes and policies inthe University’s primary governance document, and administrative and academic policyclearinghouse: the University Manual.
The committee has discussed three approved policies and onedraft policy; this report outlines concerns raised during those preliminary discussions about fourpolicies.
CBUM will continue the process of reviewing policies and reporting to the Senate anyconcerns raised during our discussions.

Given the daunting volume of policies requiring review,CBUM reiterates President Rice’s September call and requests that all other Senate standingcommittees, individual Senators, and the faculty that the Senate represents also contribute activelyand conscientiously to this effort. 1.
Policy 01.110.1.
Policy on adverse weather and other emergencies ○ Administrative vs. academic policy: As currently written, the policy is so expansive thatit extends beyond the appropriate administrative realm and includes academicmatters: such issues do not fall within the purview of the APC.
The decision to cancelclasses or to shift to a different instructional modality is not an administrative decision,but an academic one.

○ Chain of responsible people for academic decision-making: Although it may seemlogical for the chain of responsible people for decision-making to mimic the currentBoard of Trustees language about University officers, this chain does not seemappropriate or advisable in the case of academic decisions.
The University Manualcontains provisions for the Vice Provost for Academic and Faculty Initiatives torepresent the Office of the Provost in the absence of the Provost (2.22.11).
In the eventthat the Provost is unable to make a decision about class cancellation or a change ininstructional modality, the Vice Provost seems to be the most appropriateadministrator to make such decisions.
Recommended action: Revise the policy to eliminate all components relating to academics,faculty, and instructional modalities.
The Faculty Senate, not the APC, is the appropriate bodyto develop and approve academic policies. 2.

Policy 01.102.1 - External Speakers on Campus ○ On page 4, the conduct section states “If as a result of the presence or behavior of theSponsored Guest on University Property a protest, rally, or riot occurs or is threatened … the University has the right in its sole discretion at any time to revoke theSponsored Guest’s status and cancel the event.” ○ The inclusion of “presence” in addition to “behavior” suggests that the Universitycould cancel an event with a speaker who is controversial simply because people mightprotest the event, not because the speaker's actions incited a disturbance.
This seemsto conflict not only with the UM language on controversial persons (6.14.10-6.14.17),but also with precedent regarding free speech rights and the idea that the governmentmay not use a "heckler's veto" to justify suppressing speech.
Recommended action: Revise the policy to address the conflicts. 3.
Policy 02.103.2 - Graffiti - Graffiti is defined as "Unauthorized and unlawful writings or drawingsmade on a wall or other surface." This definition is so broad that it includes even something asbenign as using chalk to draw on walkways.

Recommended action: Revise the definition of graffiti in the policy. 4.
Draft policy on Research Misconduct ○ Administrative vs. academic policy: The draft policy focuses on academic research andethical conduct of academic research, and thus does not fall under the purview of theAPC. ○ Anonymous ethics hotline: The draft policy contains a section on an Ethics Hotline.Although the intent of this is understandable, there is concern that it could be used

unethically and inappropriately to target certain people or create difficulties for them.Because anonymous reports are allowed, there is potential for misuse. ○ Lack of vetting of the draft by research faculty: The Stakeholder Group that reviewedthis draft policy included only one faculty member. ○ Inclusion of the Faculty Senate among the entities that, as of October 11, 2022, had“reviewed” the draft policy: The draft policy was included on the Faculty SenateSeptember meeting agenda for the purpose of making the community aware of thevolume of policies that the APC was developing and approving and the speed at whichthe APC was doing this work. The Faculty Senate did not review, discuss, or approve thedraft policy: the Faculty Senate leadership requested that Senators, committees, andindividual members of the faculty review this draft policy (and all other policies listedon the agenda) and bring forward concerns in the future. Recommended action: Refer this draft policy in its entirety to the Faculty Senate: the FacultySenate, not the APC, is the appropriate body to work with the President, the Vice President ofResearch and Economic Development, and General Counsel to revise and legislate researchpolicies.

Goals, Activities, and Evaluation
Responsible team members are indicated in parentheses.
Illinois Computing Accelerator for Non-Specialists (iCAN)

Goal: Expand the iCAN program to 20-25 students in 2021 with at least 50% of enrolled students identifying as underrepresented in computing because of their race, gender, and/or disability status.
Activities: To broaden access to computing for people with a bachelor’s degree in any field other than CS, we created iCAN, which launched in the fall of 2020. iCAN’s mission is to broaden participation in computing through an accelerated program for non-CS college graduates. The inaugural class has 7 students, 57% of whom are from groups underrepresented in computing because of their gender and/or race. We seek to expand to 20-25 students, and apply to enable students to be eligible for federal student loans to make the program more accessible (Williams, Amato, Viswanathan).
Collect and Analyze Data: Retention
Goal: In 2020-2021, identify rates of attrition among CS majors to guide our 2021-2022 BPC Plan.
Activities: To better understand attrition within our BS programs, we will identify our attrition rates disaggregated by race, ethnicity, gender, and first-generation college status (Chacko). These data will inform the BPC plan for 2021-2022, but will not necessarily be shared.

Collect and Analyze Data: Data Buddies Survey
Goal: In 2020-2021, expand student participation in the Data Buddies Survey to at least 500 undergraduate students and 300 graduate students. (Previously 172 and 176, respectively).
Activities: To better understand our students’ experiences, we seek to increase our student’s participation in the annual Data Buddies survey, which disaggregates data by gender and race. We plan to (1) offer a raffle (Lewis), (2) promote the survey with our student groups (Coleman), (3) share email and presentation templates with faculty (Amato), and (4) promote the survey in weekly department emails that students receive (Harris). In the Spring of 2021, we will review our Data Buddies Survey report in a departmental faculty meeting.
Student Community Organization
Goal: Provide student organizations transparency into and a voice in departmental BPC efforts.

Activities: To have students’ priorities drive our BPC efforts, we have student representation on our BPC committee and we will solicit suggestions of BPC initiatives at the monthly CS Student Leadership Council (CSSLC) meetings (Coleman/Amato/Harris). We have a thriving set of student organizations that are represented at the CSSLC meetings (e.g., Blacks and African Americans in Computing, Latinxs in Computer Science, Women in Computer Science, WiCyS, AI4ALL, and Hack4Impact). At the CSSLC meetings, students will also be encouraged to attend the Department Head’s weekly open office hours to share additional suggestions. To provide transparency to students, we will also present updates from the BPC committee with particular attention to how student suggestions have shaped the committee’s work.
Faculty and Staff BPC Education
Goal: Encourage faculty and staff participation in opportunities to learn about BPC and racism.

Activities: To increase faculty and staff knowledge of BPC and racism more generally, we will encourage participation in relevant workshops and seminars. Faculty will be asked to report their participation in their annual faculty reports. In the fall of 2020, we started the monthly speaker series “Illinois Computer Science Conversations on Equity & Justice in Computing.” This supplements workshops and seminars hosted by the Office of the Vice Chancellor for Diversity, Equity, & Inclusion and the Grainger College of Engineering Institute for Inclusion, Diversity, Equity, and Access. We will promote at least one event in each “Inside CS Weekly Digest” (Harris).

4 Part I Statutes and Rules for the Government of the University Chapter 1 – The Board of Education, The Council on Postsecondary Education, and the President of the University Board of Education 1.10.10 Background.
On May 7, 1981, the Rhode Island General Assembly voted that public higher education in Rhode Island should be regulated by a body called “Board of Governors for Higher Education.” In 2012, the Rhode Island General Assembly voted that, beginning with 2013, the Board of Governors should be replaced by a Board of Education, in charge of all of public education in Rhode Island.
Administrative Report January 2017 1.10.11 Composition of the Board and Quorum Requirements.
The Board of Education is to consist of seventeen (17) public members appointed by the Governor with the advice and consent of the Rhode Island Senate.
The Chair of the Governor’s Workforce Board, or designee, and the Chair of the Rhode Island Commerce Corporation, or designee, shall serve as non-voting, ex-officio members of the board.
The Governor shall select from the appointed members a chairperson and vice chairperson.
A quorum shall consist of nine (9) members of the board.

A majority vote of those present shall be required for action.
The Chair of the Board shall have no term and shall serve at the pleasure of the governor.
Administrative Report January 2017 1.10.12 Chief Responsibility of the Board.
According to its webpage (http://www.ride.ri.gov/BoardofEducation/BoardMembers.aspx, accessed 1/5/17), “The Board of Education is the chief policy-setting body overseeing K-20 education in Rhode Island.
Through its designated powers and duties, the Board helps shape the course of public education to ensure that all of the state’s students receive the best possible education.” Administrative Report January 2017 Council on Postsecondary Education 1.20.10 Background.
In June of 2014, the Board of Education voted to establish two separate sub-councils, one being the Council on Elementary and Secondary Education, the other being the Council on Postsecondary Education.

The Council on Postsecondary Education is chiefly in charge of those matters relating to the University of Rhode Island for which university-internal approval is not sufficient. “The Council is an independent public corporation vested with the responsibility of providing oversight for the system of public higher education in Rhode Island.
This system consists of three public institutions of higher learning, the University of Rhode Island (URI), Rhode Island College (RIC), and the Community College of Rhode Island (CCRI), along with the Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner.
The Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner, which operates under the direction of the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education, is the administrative and research arm of the Rhode Island Council on Postsecondary Education.” (https://www.riopc.edu/page/Council%20overview/) Administrative Report January 2017 1.20.11 Composition of the Council.

The Council on Postsecondary Education comprises eight members appointed by the Governor from the members of the Board of Education, to serve until their terms on the Board expire, and one non- voting student member appointed for a two-year term from one of the three public Rhode Island institutions of higher learning.
The Council’s chair shall be appointed by the Governor from one of the eight voting members of the Council.
In addition, the Chair of the Board of Education shall serve on the Council in an ex officio, non-voting capacity. (see RIGL §16-59-2).
Administrative Report January 2017 1.20.12 Chief Responsibilities of the Council.

The Council’s responsibilities include (for more details, see Rhode Island General laws § 16-59-1 and § 16-59-4): (1) It shall retain all authority formerly vested in the Board of Education regarding the employment of faculty and staff at the public higher education institutions. (2) It shall prepare and maintain a five (5) year funding plan for higher education that implements the strategic financing recommendations of the Board of Education. (3) It shall prepare with the assistance of the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education and to present annually to the State Budget Officer in accordance with § 35-3-4 a state higher education budget.
Prior to submitting the budget to the State Budget Officer as required by the budget office instructions and this subsection, the Council shall

5 present the budget to the Board of Education for its review and approval. (4) It shall appoint and dismiss presidents of the public institutions of higher learning with the assistance of the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education, and to establish procedures for this, and with the assistance of the Commissioner to approve or disapprove vice presidents of the public institutions of higher learning appointed by the respective presidents of the public institutions of higher learning. (5) It shall delegate to the presidents of each public higher education institution the authority and responsibility for operational and management decisions related to their institutions, consistent with the goals of the statewide strategic plan for postsecondary education, provided however that the presidents may be required to provide information or updates to the council regarding any delegated operational or management decisions.
Administrative Report January 2017 The President of the University 1.30.10 Presidential Powers—Shared Governance.

In 2014, the President of the University received authority over certain items that previously needed to be submitted for approval to the super-ordinated state body (Board of Governors, Board of Regents, etc.).
The items over which the President now has authority include: “To create, and consolidate departments, divisions, programs, and courses of study within the university with the assistance of the commissioner of postsecondary education within the approved role and scope adopted by the council on postsecondary education pursuant to § 16-59-4” (See RI General Law § 16-32-2.1).

The law stipulates, however, that this authority is to be exercised “consistent with shared governance practices, [and] in conformity with § 16-32-10,” which states that it “shall also be the duty of the president and a committee of the faculty, . . . to arrange courses of study conforming to all acts of Congress, and prescribe any qualifications for the admission of students and any rules of study, exercise, discipline, and government as the president and committee may deem proper.” For more than half a century, the committee of the faculty mentioned in this legislation has been understood to be the URI Faculty Senate.

Should the Ombudsman arrive at conclusions which are critical of the operations and practices of the office of the President, or of the Presidential disposition of cases duly reported by the Ombudsman to the President, s/he shall so inform the President; and if there is no resolution of the problem which is satisfactory to him/her

11 the Ombudsman may take the matter directly to the Chairperson of the Board of Education, informing the President before s/he does so. 2.39.16 Powers of the Ombudsman shall include: access to all records pertinent to any allegation of inequity or injustice or other grievance coming under his/her jurisdiction; the right to inquire of any officer of instruction or of administration, or of any member of the clerical and custodial staffs, or of any student, in connection with his/her proper inquiries and to receive full and complete answers; the right to mediate or otherwise arrive at a compromise or to arrive at his/her own proposal for solution of the problem at hand; the right to present his/her recommendations for solution to the parties involved and to report such recommendations to the supervisory officers of the person(s) involved and to the office of the President and to the Chairperson of the Faculty Senate; and having completed the foregoing process in confidence the right to make a final public report on the matter. 2.39.17 The Ombudsman shall be provided with office facilities by the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs including part-time secretarial help. 2.39.18 Compensation and Release Time.

If the nominee is a full-time faculty member, his/her teaching and/or research load shall be adjusted in consultation with his/her departmental chairperson, his/her dean, and the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs.
Every effort shall be made to reduce his/her teaching and research load appropriately and professional expectations for accomplishment in these areas shall reflect this commitment to the position of Ombudsman.
S/he shall be free of all committee assignments, student advising and other similar duties, during his/her term of office.
The faculty member’s department shall be provided with replacement funding from the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs to the extent of one course per semester.
Any additional release time for a full-time faculty member, shall be negotiated by the nominee with the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs before Faculty Senate confirmation.
The summer retainer and any compensation for an emeritus faculty member shall be provided by the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs. 2.39.19 Student Assistant.

The Ombudsman shall be assisted by a student appointed by the President by July 1 each year in accordance with the procedure outlined below.
In March of each academic year, the Student Senate and Graduate Student Association shall conduct searches for their nominees to the position of Student Assistant to the Ombudsman.
The searches shall be conducted in a manner established by each organization.
The names of no more than three nominees from each group shall be forwarded to the current Ombudsman by April 15.
Finalists for the position shall be interviewed by a committee composed of the Ombudsman and a representative of the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs.
The committee shall be convened by the Ombudsman and shall make its recommendation to the President no later than June 15.
The Ombudsman’s Student Assistant shall perform his/her duties in consultation with and under the direction of the Ombudsman, shall serve a one-year term, and shall be eligible to succeed himself/herself without a search.
The Ombudsman’s Student Assistant shall receive a stipend of $1000 per semester, to be paid by the University. #03-04–23 2.39.20 Conflict of Interest.

If a complaint to the Ombudsman in any way compromises the objectivity of the Ombudsman in handling the case, a past Ombudsman may be called upon to serve on an ad hoc basis.
